output.title: What capacity limits usually hide
output.body:
Capacity limits are often not a vague “we need AI” problem. They show up in one repeatable workflow decision: do you keep answering the same customer questions by hand, or do you build a bounded system that handles the routine part and leaves judgment with you? For a small business owner, that is usually the real comparison: another hire, more manual work, or a narrow automation investment.

A useful test is simple. Are most of these requests coming from a small set of common patterns, or is every case genuinely different? If the work is mostly repeatable, AI can help with the standard part. If each case needs live judgment, context, or a human call, then forcing automation is the wrong move. That is not a failure; it is just a boundary.

Bareni’s next step is not to “AI everything.” It is to identify one recurring workflow, check whether it fits, and then define a small pilot only if it does. In practice, that means scope, fixed price, and measures. It does not mean promising outcomes. Human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions, and finished code is handed over with accounts in the customer’s name as policy.

That is usually what capacity limits hide: a bottleneck in one boring process that keeps landing on the desk. Start there, and keep the rest human.
